fatal_errors: The proposed PVD coating is not compositionally specified, so neither its low-temperature ceramic behavior nor its high-temperature lubricious oxidation products are scientifically testable.
The intervention misses the target strategy of varying Mo content in a Ni/MoS2-Ag-Cr2O3-containing CoCrFeNiMox composite.
The cited evidence supports generic tribo-oxide formation but does not establish that a graded PVD coating on CoCrFeNi can maintain low friction and wear from room temperature to 800 °C.
The proposed 10–30 N load range and 20 N experiment do not reproduce the relevant 8 N test condition and make comparison with the target behavior unreliable.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the broad wide-temperature tribology problem and offers a controlled coated-versus-uncoated comparison, but it does not reconstruct the reported materials design. It omits Mo-induced FCC lattice distortion, sigma-phase strengthening, Ni/MoS2 and Ag low-temperature lubrication, and silver-molybdate/NiO glaze formation at high temperature. Its pristine-alloy baseline also differs from the Mo0.2 composite baseline. The mechanism is only a generic hard-coating-to-oxide-glaze narrative, with no coating chemistry, architecture, deposition parameters, counterface, speed, distance, or temperature-specific predictions. The experiment could test an adequately specified coating, but as written it cannot connect particular phases to performance, and incremental heating may confound temperature with accumulated wear and thermal history. Evidence E1 and E3 supports oxide-glaze lubrication in general, while E2 primarily highlights oxidation-induced porosity and cracking; none directly validates the central graded-PVD intervention. Thus the proposal is conceivable but insufficiently specified and supported to qualify as a well-supported plausible alternative.
